analysis.time: Published on July 24, 2026. Event timeframe not specified, but the rise in wildlife encounters is described as recent.
analysis.location_and_population: Chatham-Kent, Ontario, Canada. General public, with emphasis on residents and children.
analysis.event: Chatham-Kent Public Health (CKPH) reported an increase in preventable wildlife encounters with bats and raccoons, leading to a rise in Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) treatments. The event is confirmed as a public health precautionary notice.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Cases of human rabies are rare but treatable with timely intervention. A growing number of people have required PEP. The risk is explicitly stated as preventable by avoiding direct contact with wildlife.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: CKPH is advising the public to admire wildlife from a distance and avoid contact. Precautions include not touching wild animals, keeping pets vaccinated, and seeking medical attention after exposure. Potential exposures should be reported to CKPH for assessment. The source is a full original report with no unresolved information.

analysis.brief_en: Chatham-Kent Public Health has issued precautionary tips following an increase in wildlife encounters with bats and raccoons, leading to more people requiring Rabies Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP). While human rabies cases are rare and treatable with timely medical intervention, officials emphasize that avoiding direct contact with wildlife is the best protection. The health unit advises residents to admire animals from a distance, never touch or feed them, ensure pets are vaccinated, and seek professional help for sick or injured wildlife. Those bitten, scratched, or in direct contact with a bat should wash the area thoroughly and seek immediate medical attention, while also reporting potential exposures to CKPH for follow-up.

While human rabies cases are rare and treatable with timely medical intervention, officials emphasize that avoiding direct contact with wildlife is the best protection. The health unit advises residents to admire animals from a distance, never touch or feed them, ensure pets are vaccinated, and seek professional help for sick or injured wildlife. Those bitten, scratched, or in direct contact with a bat should wash the area thoroughly and seek immediate medical attention, while also reporting potential exposures to CKPH for follow-up.

By Pranati Kotamraju • Published July 23, 2026 • Updated on July 24, 2026 at 12:59 pm Log in or create a free profile to save articlesBOOKMARKER 0:00Pause0:00 / 0:58UnmuteSubtitlesEnglishNoneSettingsShareToggle Fullscreenestimates that any given night. Get this. There are as many as NBC Universal, Inc. Local health officials say a bat that tested positive for rabies landed on the table of a restaurant while a family was eating. Now, they have a warning for anyone who may have touched it. San Diego County officials are looking for anyone who may have come in direct contact with a rabid bat after it flew into a Vista restaurant on Sunday. The incident occurred at 1 p.m. on July 19 at the Yellow Deli Restaurant, when a family was eating dinner and a bat landed on their table. Another diner picked up the bat using a towel and brought it to the Humane Society in Oceanside. Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7. WATCH HERE After being brought to the county’s public health lab, the bat tested positive for rabies, but as of Thursday, there have been no reports of people coming into direct contact with the bat, according to the county. Health officials warn any individuals who may have come in direct contact with the bat to call their health care provider immediately. "Rabies has nearly a 100% fatality rate if treatment is not obtained prior to symptoms starting. So you need to seek care before symptoms start, or there is no treatment for rabies, unfortunately," said Emily Trumbull, a veterinarian for the county of San Diego’s Epidemiology Unit. This is the 22nd bat to test positive for rabies in San Diego County this year, as there has been an increased number of human and bat interactions this year--- but it doesn’t directly correlate to more bats having rabies, Trumbull said. “We work closely with animal health partners throughout the county to monitor for rabies among a variety of species,” Trumbull said. “We test animals that may be suspicious for rabies, or that could be putting someone at high risk because of the type of exposure they had to these animals. (KOLO) - The Nevada Department of Agriculture is urging residents to vaccinate their pets against rabies.They say that since the start of the year, their Animal Disease Laboratory has identified three bats in Lyon, White Pine and Clark counties that have tested positive for rabies.“Rabies can be effectively controlled with proper vaccination,” said NDA State Veterinarian Dr. Peter Rolfe, DVM. “Keeping pets up to date on vaccines is the best way to protect both animals and the people around them.”The deadly virus can affect dogs, cats, livestock and humans. Bats are active in the state of Nevada between May and October and can enter homes or barns undetected.“Annual monitoring in Nevada continues to identify bats that test positive for rabies, reinforcing the need for preventive care,” added Laura Morrow, NDA Animal Disease Laboratory supervisor. “Testing helps us track where the virus is present and provide information to the public and animal health agencies, supporting their response to potential exposures.” Nevada law requires owners to vaccinate their dogs, cats and ferrets to be vaccinated against rabies. Vaccines are also available for certain kinds of livestock.“Maintaining current rabies vaccinations for pets and avoiding direct contact with wildlife are critical steps in reducing risk,” said NDA Director J.J. Goicoechea, DVM. “Bats, in particular, should never be handled, as they can carry rabies even when no obvious signs of illness are present.”Copyright 2026 KOLO. news.content_title: Rabid Bat Found Near Safari Park Restaurant Prompts Health Warning
news.content: This is an undated closeup photo of the eastern pipistrelle bat, a species that is frequently linked with human rabies cases. (Merlin D./The Canadian Press/AP) A bat found dead outside a restaurant at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park has tested positive for rabies, prompting county health officials to seek out anyone who may have touched the animal. The bat was found at 12:10 p.m. on July 11 at the Oasis on the Rocks restaurant inside the Safari Park, according to the county. A trained park employee collected the animal, and officials said no human contact with the bat has been reported so far, according to a recent San Diego County News Center press release . County officials stressed that the bat was not part of the park's animal collection. The specimen was taken to the County Public Health Laboratory on July 13, where testing confirmed rabies. Health Officials Seek Close Contacts County Public Health Services is asking anyone who had direct contact with the bat—including touching or holding it—or who knows someone who may have, to call (619) 692-8499 immediately. Officials noted that only people with direct physical contact face any risk of infection. "We are investigating to ensure anyone who came into contact with the bat receives care quickly. Once symptoms start there is no treatment for rabies," Kadakia said. Latest In A String Of Cases This marks the 19th bat to test positive for rabies in San Diego County so far this year. That figure trails the 21 rabid bats recorded in all of 2025. County health officials reiterated standard precautions: avoid touching bats or any wildlife, and wash any exposed skin with soap and seek medical advice immediately after contact with a bat. Rabies symptoms can take weeks or months to surface, but the disease is almost always fatal once symptoms begin. Human rabies cases remain rare. California's most recent human case was recorded in 2024, when a Fresno County resident was exposed to a bat in Merced County. Officials noted that bats serve an important ecological role in San Diego County, feeding on insects like mosquitoes and pollinating plants through nectar feeding. Velez - 5 hours ago Personnel from the Malaybalay City Veterinary Office prepare a large net to catch a stray dog during a “Dakip-Aso” operation. The city government has intensified its stray-catching drive across all barangays under Republic Act 9482 (Anti-Rabies Act of 2007) to curb rabies cases, bite incidents, and street accidents. (Photo by LGU Malaybalay City) MALAYBALAY CITY, Bukidnon — The city government recently intensified its citywide “Dakip-Aso” campaign against stray dogs across all barangays, resulting in 33 dogs euthanized, 44 impounded, 10 reclaimed by their owners and one adopted. The initiative strictly enforces Republic Act No. 9482, or the Anti-Rabies Act of 2007. Local authorities aim to eliminate human rabies fatalities, reduce animal bite incidents, and minimize road accidents caused by unconfined pets. Teams equipped with nets and transport vehicles are patrolling local thoroughfares to impound roaming animals. City veterinarian Jude Ignatius Casimero stated that free-roaming animals have increased public road accidents and bite incidents, resulting in greater demand on the local government for medical and financial assistance. Captured animals are taken to the city veterinary facility where they receive temporary shelter, food, vaccinations and basic care. Under city guidelines, pet owners have three days to retrieve impounded animals after paying a P1,100 penalty. Unclaimed animals are offered for adoption. The unadopted ones undergo humane euthanasia as a final resort. Malaybalay City Mayor Jay Warren Pabillaran reminded owners to keep pets leashed or confined to private property and encouraged participation in free government vaccination programs. “Enforcing the Anti-Rabies Act is not just about impounding stray animals—it is a vital measure to protect our citizens, especially children, from rabies while ensuring pet owners take full responsibility for their animals,” Pabillaran said. news.source_body_en: Malaybalay City has intensified its citywide 'Dakip-Aso' campaign against stray dogs to curb rabies cases, bite incidents, and road accidents. Under Republic Act 9482, the initiative has resulted in 33 dogs euthanized, 44 impounded, 10 reclaimed, and 1 adopted. Captured animals receive care at the city veterinary facility, with owners given three days to reclaim them after a P1,100 penalty. Mayor Jay Warren Pabillaran emphasized the importance of enforcing the Anti-Rabies Act to protect citizens, especially children, while urging pet owners to keep pets confined and participate in free vaccination programs.

Health officials say never touch a bat and call PACC if one enters your home. Prev Next Pima County bat exposures have hit a record high. Here's what health officials say you should do if you encounter one. By: Vanessa Gongora Posted 5:25 AM, Jul 24, 2026 and last updated 6:07 PM, Jul 24, 2026 TUCSON, Ariz. — It’s the time of year when bats are seen throughout Pima County, and it is a fascinating experience where many people go to nearby bridges and wait for them to come out at sunset. You always want to make sure you keep your distance.Tucson Medical Center's (TMC) emergency department has seen a significant spike in patients seeking treatment for bat exposure, and Pima County health officials say the number of bat-related animal exposures has already surpassed 2025's peak on record. 1/1 Skip Ad Continue watchingafter the adVisit Advertiser websiteGO TO PAGETMC's Pediatric Emergency Department Manager Hannah Gerbracht said the hospital has treated about 20 patients in the last week alone, administering rabies vaccines as a precaution."We obviously do an assessment. Ask what the bats looked like, were they awake, were they acting weird, and then we do prophylactically treat everybody who comes into the ER with rabies vaccines and immunoglobulin," Gerbracht said.Gerbracht said bat exposures don't always mean you were necessarily bitten, but you were close in proximity. "Whether that means bats in their house or in a pool that they've been in, but we've seen a great deal over the last probably three weeks, coming in for bats in their houses," Gerbracht said.The Pima County Health Department (PCHD) has dealt with194 bats exposed to people so far this year. Dr. Ellen Santos, PCHD's Epidemiology Program Manager, said July's numbers are already skyrocketing. PCHD "So this black dotted line here, this is the number of animal exposures in people that we dealt with last year, so in 2025. And so we peaked in August, but you can see for July, and the month's not even over yet, we are above any peak that we've seen," Dr. Santos said.Health officials urge the public never to touch a bat, whether it is dead or alive. If a pet has a bat in its mouth, Santos said, stay protected when trying to remove it. "If your dog brings in a bat from outside, you know, try to get it away from your dog with like, you know, a plastic, some sort of barrier or gloves or something," Dr. Santos said. "And then call your veterinarian to do an assessment for your animal," Dr. Santos said.If a bat is found inside a home, residents can call Pima Animal Care Center (PACC) to retrieve it. The bat will then be tested for rabies, and the results will determine whether the people in the home need to seek medical care."What usually happens is if someone encounters a bat or a wild animal, they will call us, or it'll get reported to us somehow, and we will reach out to that person, and we'll ask them a whole bunch of questions about what happened and all that is to help us determine, is this a low risk situation, is this a high risk situation? And for anything that is kind of moderate or high risk, we might recommend seeking healthcare," Dr. Santos said. She said there are visible signs that a bat may be infected with rabies."Some symptoms you might see if the bat does have rabies and is symptomatic, they might be kind of flying around during the day when we don't expect to see them. They might appear kind of sick," Santos said. "You might find them on the ground, kind of flopping around. You might find them kind of moving around in a way that you wouldn't expect them to be flying. So, any kind of unusual-looking behavior is usually suspicious."One patient treated at TMC found a bat in their pool. Dr. Santos said residents in that situation do not need to drain the pool."Even if that bat has rabies, the rabies virus is very fragile in the environment, so exposure to things like sun, sunlight, UV light outside of a warm-blooded animal, a mammal, that rabies virus is not going to survive," Santos said. "But if anyone encountered that bat, like physically touched it, or, you know, if the bat flew at them and they notice a bite or a scratch, that's when we would want to do an assessment, and we'd be a little more concerned."She says one thing to remember about bats is that they are really tiny, as well as their teeth, so if a bat bites you, you don't always see it or know that it's there."So that's why if you wake up at home and you notice that a bat has been flying around, that we consider a high-risk situation because while you're asleep or not aware of what's going on, we don't know if that bat came up to you or bit because those bites are so tiny," Dr. Santos said.Bats are a protected species, and there are several popular locations in the area to observe them. analysis.time: Published on July 24, 2026. Event occurred in July 2026, with a spike in the last week and over the past three weeks.
analysis.location_and_population: Pima County, Arizona, USA. Affected population includes residents who encountered bats, with specific locations mentioned: East Broadway bridge over the Pantano Wash, North Campbell Avenue bridge over the Rillito, East Tanque Verde bridge over the Rillito, and Ina Road bridge at the Santa Cruz River.
analysis.event: Record high number of bat exposures in Pima County, Arizona, in July 2026. Tucson Medical Center treated about 20 patients in the last week for bat exposure, and Pima County Health Department reported 194 bat exposures to people so far in 2026, surpassing 2025's peak. Health officials confirmed the increase and provided guidance on handling bat encounters.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 194 bat exposures to people reported in Pima County so far in 2026, with July's numbers already exceeding the previous year's peak. Tucson Medical Center treated approximately 20 patients in the last week. Risk includes potential rabies transmission, though bites may not always be visible due to bats' small size. Health officials classify situations as low, moderate, or high risk based on exposure details.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health officials are investigating and responding to the spike in bat exposures. Tucson Medical Center administers rabies vaccines and immunoglobulin as a precaution. Pima County Health Department assesses each case to determine risk level and recommends medical care for moderate or high-risk exposures. Bats are tested for rabies, and results guide further action. Public is advised to never touch bats, call Pima Animal Care Center if a bat is in their home, and seek medical attention if exposed. Uncertainty remains regarding the exact cause of the increased bat activity.

analysis.brief_en: Pima County, Arizona, is experiencing a record number of bat exposures in July 2026, with health officials reporting a significant spike surpassing previous years' peaks. Tucson Medical Center has treated about 20 patients in the last week alone, administering rabies vaccines as a precaution. The Pima County Health Department has documented 194 bat exposures to people so far this year, with July's numbers already exceeding the 2025 peak. Health officials urge the public to never touch bats, whether dead or alive, and to call the Pima Animal Care Center if a bat enters their home. Bats are tested for rabies, and results determine if medical care is needed. The rabies virus is fragile in the environment, but physical contact or bites require assessment. Residents are advised to observe bats from a distance and report unusual behavior, such as daytime activity or appearing sick.

news.content_title: Lake County confirms first rabid bat in 4 years
news.content: PAINESVILLE, Ohio — The Lake County General Health District announced Thursday that a bat from Painesville tested positive for rabies. A resident reported the bat, which was found in their home. It's the first rabid bat to be confirmed rabid in the county since 2022. "Bats are beneficial, as they eat large numbers of flying insects, but bats may also be a source of rabies," said LCGHD Environmental Health Supervisor Bert Mechenbier. Mechenbier said humans and pets can get the virus if they are either bitten or scratched by an infected animal. It can also happen when saliva from an infected animal gets into an open wound. Despite this, Health Commissioner Adam Litke said people should not worry. "Residents should not fear spending time outside, but should be aware and keep their pets nearby," Litke said. Those who believe they may have been exposed to rabies should seek immediate medical attention. Individuals will go through a process called post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) which includes wound care, human rabies immune globulin and a series of four or five rabies vaccines, which must be given as soon as possible after exposure, according to the department. The process is nearly 100% effective. If Ohioans find a bat in their homes, they're encouraged to take the following steps: - Close all windows and doors, and leave the bat in the room - Call a professional to capture the bat - If there is no professional to capture the bat, Miami County Public Health recommends putting on leather gloves, slowly approaching the bat when it lands, and placing a see-through container over the bat. Then, slide a lid under the container to trap the bat. Secure the lid with tape and punch small holes in the container to allow the bat to breathe. So far this year, there have been 15 confirmed rabies cases in Ohio and all from bats — not including this recent confirmation in Lake County, according to the Ohio Department of Health. In mid-May, that number stood at seven. In 2025, there were 19 confirmed cases of bats with rabies across the state, a sharp decline from 2024, which had 43. In Ohio, there are more than 20,000 bite exposures and 1,000 non-bite exposures are reported in Ohio each year, exposing more than 21,000 people, according to ODH. Non-bite exposures can happen when a bat is found in a room with a child, someone who is sleeping or someone with a sensory or mental impairment

news.content: Health officials issue dire warning to unsuspecting restaurant guests possibly exposed to rabies See more of our coverage in your search results. Add The California Post on GoogleLunch with a side of rabid bat. A rabid bat landed on a munching family’s table at a San Diego deli restaurant this past Sunday. San Diego public health officials are concerned, issuing a notice to anyone who may have touched the bat that they are at risk of contracting rabies and should call their healthcare provider. No direct contact with the bat was reported. A diner scooped up the bat with a towel and transported it to the Humane Society in Oceanside, where it tested positive for the highly fatal disease. The bat is the 22nd to test positive for rabies in San Diego County this year, already beating 2025’s 21 rabid bats. It’s the most confirmed rabies-positive bats since at least 2021, according to county data. Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter California's top news, sports and entertainment delivered to your inbox every day. Thanks for signing up! Bats are the only species to test positive for rabies this year. San Diego officials reminded residents: - Respect the space of wildlife, do not touch or approach bats or any wildlife. - If you have direct contact with a bat, wash the exposed area with soap and seek medical advice. - Rabies symptoms can take weeks to months to appear, and once symptoms begin, the disease is almost always fatal. Prompt treatment after an exposure is highly effective. The state hasn’t had a human rabies case since 2024, when a Fresno County resident was exposed to a rabid bat in Merced County. Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms are seen but is considered preventable with treatment. San Diego officials emphasized the importance of bats in the local ecosystem. “Bats play an important role in our local ecosystem,” they wrote. “Many species of bats live in San Diego County, feeding on insects such as mosquitos. Other bat species feed on nectar from plants and pollinate them in the process. You may see bats occasionally around sunset when they are most active. It is important to respect wildlife and give wild animals space to play their role in our natural environment. ” What do you think? Post a comment. Fewer than 10 Americans die from rabies every year, according to the CDC. It’s unclear what the bat ordered, but the family hopes the flying mammal is not giving them any leftovers to take home. news.content_title: Health Warning Issued for Unsuspecting Diners After Bat Tests Positive for Rabies
news.content: A pallid bat flying over a pond at night in a file photo. (Shutterstock) San Diego County health officials are asking anyone who may have handled a bat that landed on a table at a Vista restaurant last weekend to seek medical attention after lab tests confirmed the animal was infected with rabies. The bat appeared at the Yellow Deli Restaurant in Vista at 1 p.m. Sunday, July 19, landing on a table while a family was dining, the County of San Diego Communications Office said Thursday. Another customer used a towel to capture the animal and brought it to the Humane Society in Oceanside, which then transferred it to the County's Public Health Lab, where testing confirmed rabies. County officials said no direct skin contact with the bat has been reported so far. Still, anyone who touched or held the animal, or who knows someone who may have, is being urged to contact a health care provider immediately, since only people with direct physical contact face any risk of infection. Health officials said that rabies post-exposure prophylaxis works well when administered before symptoms appear, but once symptoms set in, there is no treatment and the disease is almost always fatal. The Vista incident is the 22nd bat to test positive for rabies in San Diego County this year, surpassing the 21 rabid bats recorded in all of 2025. That tally builds on a case reported just days earlier, when a bat found dead outside the Oasis on the Rocks restaurant at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park tested positive for rabies after being collected by a park employee on July 11. That bat was confirmed as the 19th of the year. Two earlier rabid bats were also found in March near Escondido's White Oak Villas condo complex and at the Safari Park's Okavango Restaurant. "Rabies is an extremely serious viral disease, one of the deadliest, with nearly 100% fatality if not caught early enough," said Dr. Ankita Kadakia, the county's deputy public health officer, in an announcement following the earlier incident. "We are investigating to ensure anyone who came into contact with the bat receives care quickly. Once symptoms start there is no treatment for rabies.” County Public Health Services continues to urge residents to avoid touching or approaching bats or any wildlife, and to wash any exposed skin with soap and seek medical advice immediately after contact. Rabies symptoms can take weeks to months to appear, but the illness is almost always fatal once symptoms begin. Human rabies cases remain rare. California's most recent human case occurred in 2024, involving a Fresno County resident exposed to a bat in Merced County. Despite the recent cases, officials noted bats play an important ecological role in San Diego County, feeding on insects such as mosquitoes and pollinating plants by feeding on nectar. Residents may spot bats around sunset, when they are most active, and officials asked the public to give the animals space. Anyone with questions about a possible exposure or rabies prevention can contact the county's Epidemiology unit at (619) 692-8499. Conversation Conversations are moderated. news.content_original: A pallid bat flying over a pond at night in a file photo. (Shutterstock) San Diego County health officials are asking anyone who may have handled a bat that landed on a table at a Vista restaurant last weekend to seek medical attention after lab tests confirmed the animal was infected with rabies. The bat appeared at the Yellow Deli Restaurant in Vista at 1 p.m. Sunday, July 19, landing on a table while a family was dining, the County of San Diego Communications Office said Thursday. Another customer used a towel to capture the animal and brought it to the Humane Society in Oceanside, which then transferred it to the County's Public Health Lab, where testing confirmed rabies. County officials said no direct skin contact with the bat has been reported so far. Still, anyone who touched or held the animal, or who knows someone who may have, is being urged to contact a health care provider immediately, since only people with direct physical contact face any risk of infection. Health officials said that rabies post-exposure prophylaxis works well when administered before symptoms appear, but once symptoms set in, there is no treatment and the disease is almost always fatal. The Vista incident is the 22nd bat to test positive for rabies in San Diego County this year, surpassing the 21 rabid bats recorded in all of 2025. That tally builds on a case reported just days earlier, when a bat found dead outside the Oasis on the Rocks restaurant at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park tested positive for rabies after being collected by a park employee on July 11. That bat was confirmed as the 19th of the year. Two earlier rabid bats were also found in March near Escondido's White Oak Villas condo complex and at the Safari Park's Okavango Restaurant. "Rabies is an extremely serious viral disease, one of the deadliest, with nearly 100% fatality if not caught early enough," said Dr. Ankita Kadakia, the county's deputy public health officer, in an announcement following the earlier incident. "We are investigating to ensure anyone who came into contact with the bat receives care quickly. Once symptoms start there is no treatment for rabies.” County Public Health Services continues to urge residents to avoid touching or approaching bats or any wildlife, and to wash any exposed skin with soap and seek medical advice immediately after contact. Rabies symptoms can take weeks to months to appear, but the illness is almost always fatal once symptoms begin. Human rabies cases remain rare. California's most recent human case occurred in 2024, involving a Fresno County resident exposed to a bat in Merced County. Despite the recent cases, officials noted bats play an important ecological role in San Diego County, feeding on insects such as mosquitoes and pollinating plants by feeding on nectar. Residents may spot bats around sunset, when they are most active, and officials asked the public to give the animals space. Anyone with questions about a possible exposure or rabies prevention can contact the county's Epidemiology unit at (619) 692-8499. Conversation Conversations are moderated. news.content: Local Sports High School Huddle Scene Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals LOCALWNC wildlife rehabilitator disputes laws after raccoons euthanized Kara FohnerAsheville Citizen TimesUpdated July 23, 2026, 9:57 a.m. ETA wildlife rehabilitator in Asheville was charged after five raccoons were seized from her facility.The operator did not have the required state permit to possess rabies vector species like raccoons.Health officials advised anyone who visited the facility in the last six months to get a rabies risk assessment.ASHEVILLE - A licensed wildlife rehabilitation operator in West Asheville found herself at odds with North Carolina wildlife laws after she rescued baby raccoons, which were later seized and euthanized by the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission.Michelle Cole, operator of Alleyoop Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation on Sand Hill Road, told the Citizen Times July 17 that she obtained the five raccoons that were seized last fall, when they were babies."They came to me when they were four weeks old, eyes still closed, four of them did. The other one was about five weeks old, and it had had its arm chopped off with a chainsaw," she said. "So, I bottle fed them, raised them. ... They've all had their rabies shots and their distemper shots."In the State of North Carolina, licensed wildlife rehabilitators must have a captivity license for rehabilitation, along with an additional rabies vector species certification, Buncombe County said in a July 16 news release. They also must have a complete rabies pre-exposure series of vaccines to be allowed to handle and rehabilitate animal species that are at high risk of carrying rabies virus, which includes bats, raccoons, skunks, foxes, and bobcats. In Buncombe County and other counties where the US Department of Agriculture’s Oral Rabies Vaccination program is conducted, the rehabilitation and release of rabies vector species is not authorized, except for bats.Cole said that she initially reached out to the N.C. Wildlife Resources Commission and asked how rabies vector species should be handled, although she didn't tell them she had rescued raccoons. She said she didn't at first know about Buncombe County's policy, but she said she was told by state officials that she was "supposed to walk away and let them die.""I'm not going to kill them. I already had them. I was really looking for what to do with them, if I could take them somewhere," she said. Cole feels the policy in Buncombe County is cruel, and so she kept the raccoons, with plans to release them into the wild when they were fully rehabilitated. Recently, she said someone she thought was a friend came over and saw one of the raccoons. That person reported her to wildlife officials."It's ludicrous, really. No one knew about them. ... No one ever went back there except me, and I've had my pre-exposure shots," she said.Cole was charged July 13 with possession of a rabies vector species without a permit, the N.C. Wildlife Resources Commission told the Citizen Times July 16.The raccoons were seized and euthanized, according to the Wildlife Resources Commission."Five raccoons (an RVS) were found being held unlawfully in captivity. The raccoons were captured, secured, and placed into carriers by agency staff with Ms. Cole’s cooperation and assistance," the organization said in a statement July 22. "The animals were euthanized following RVS/ORV rabies prevention program guidance. The consequences to wildlife are extremely difficult for everyone when laws are not followed."Wildlife law enforcement leadership reviewed body camera footage of enforcement actions taken by the officer during the seizure of the raccoons and confirmed that protocol was properly followed, the Wildlife Resources Commission added.Cole feels the laws around rabies vector species are unfair."Me and my fellow colleagues have tried to make changes with Raleigh regarding this law. They don't care. They don't listen. How do you fight the state on a moral issue? If I had money, it'd be one thing. All of my money goes into saving these animals," she said.She said that the raccoons that were seized had been vaccinated against rabies."They had their shots. If the reasoning is that they were euthanized because of the possibility of rabies, they were contained for a year, they obviously didn't have rabies," she said. "They were given their shots, and they were never introduced to the public. No one ever touched them but me."The N.C. Wildlife Resources Commission said that the investigation into Cole's facility is ongoing. In a statement, N.C. Wildlife said that while Cole has a valid rehabilitator license, she was not permitted to hold rabies vector species longer than 24 hours. The Buncombe County Department of Health and Human Services warned the public in a press release July 16 that anyone who visited the facility in the last six months should obtain a rabies risk assessment. The North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission said that the press release was a precautionary measure.Kara Fohner is the Public Safety Reporter for the Asheville Citizen Times. analysis.time: Published on July 23, 2026. The event occurred in late 2025 when the raccoons were seized, with charges filed on July 13, 2026.
analysis.location_and_population: West Asheville, North Carolina, specifically at Alleyoop Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation on Sand Hill Road. The affected population includes visitors to the facility in the last six months, who were advised to seek a rabies risk assessment.
analysis.event: A licensed wildlife rehabilitator, Michelle Cole, was charged with possession of rabies vector species without a permit after five raccoons were seized and euthanized by the North Carolina Wildlife Resources Commission. Cole disputes the laws, claiming she followed proper vaccination protocols and was unaware of specific county policies.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The Buncombe County Department of Health and Human Services issued a warning for visitors to the facility to obtain a rabies risk assessment, though the Wildlife Resources Commission called this a precautionary measure. No human rabies cases were reported.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The investigation into Cole's facility is ongoing. Wildlife officials followed protocol during the seizure, and the euthanasia was conducted per rabies prevention program guidelines. Cole maintains the raccoons were vaccinated and posed no rabies risk, but state law prohibits holding rabies vector species longer than 24 hours without proper certification.

analysis.brief_en: In West Asheville, North Carolina, licensed wildlife rehabilitator Michelle Cole faces charges after five raccoons were seized and euthanized by state officials. Cole, operator of Alleyoop Wildlife Rescue and Rehabilitation, rescued the baby raccoons last fall but lacked the required rabies vector species permit. Despite vaccinating the animals, state law prohibits holding such species longer than 24 hours without certification. The raccoons were euthanized per rabies prevention guidelines, prompting Cole to dispute the laws as cruel. news.content: News Sports Ticket Lifestyle Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals SARASOTARabid raccoon prompts Sarasota County health advisoryHealth officials urge Sarasota County residents and visitors to avoid wild animals after a confirmed rabies case. Michaela GalliganSarasota Herald-TribuneJuly 23, 2026, 11:26 a.m. ETThe Florida Department of Health in Sarasota County (DOH-Sarasota) is warning residents and visitors to be aware of rabies among wild animals in the area.A press release says the health department is monitoring a single confirmed case of rabies in a raccoon. The animal was killed on the corner of Grove Point Boulevard and Proctor Road on Tuesday, July 21. DOH says that people and domestic animals should always avoid contact with wild animals such as raccoons, bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats and coyotes, as they carry a higher risk of human rabies exposure and a need for post-exposure treatment. The department says that if a person is exposed to rabies, getting the appropriate treatment after exposure will protect them from the risk of rabies.DOH-Sarasota recommends taking the following precautions to prevent rabies exposure:Immunize pets and livestock based on a veterinarian’s recommended schedule.Keep pets under direct supervision and on a leash, and keep livestock secured on your property. If an animal bites your pet or livestock, seek veterinary assistance for the animal immediately and contact Sarasota Animal Services at 941-861-9501.Avoid contact with wild or stray animals. Do not handle, feed or unintentionally attract them with outdoor pet food, open garbage cans or other sources of food. If you have been bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal, seek medical attention, and report the injury to DOH-Sarasota by calling 941-861-2873.Never adopt wild animals or bring them into your home; instead, contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator.Call your local animal control agency to remove any stray animals from your neighborhood. You can contact Sarasota Animal Services at 941-861-9501.Prevent wildlife, including bats, from entering living quarters or occupied spaces in homes, schools and other similar areas where they might come in contact with people and pets.DOH provides additional information on rabies at FloridaHealth.gov/Rabies. You can also contact DOH-Sarasota at 941-861-2873.Michaela Galligan is an intern covering a variety of topics for the Sarasota Herald-Tribune. She can be reached at MGalligan@usatodayco.com. news.content_title: Rabid bat confirmed in Painesville, first in Lake County since 2022
news.content: MENTOR , Ohio (WJW) — A bat recently found in a Painesville home was confirmed to be infected with the rabies virus, Lake County General Health District announced on Thursday, July 23. It’s the first confirmed case of a rabid bat in Lake County since 2022, according to a news release. “Bats are beneficial, as they eat large numbers of flying insects; but bats may also be a source of rabies,” health district Supervisor Bert Mechenbier is quoted in the release. New measles cases, possible exposures in Ashtabula County Humans and pets can become infected when bitten or scratched by an infected animal or — less commonly — when saliva from an infected animal enters an open wound or a mucous membrane like the eye or inner cheek. Residents who are exposed to bats or wake up to find a bat in the house should carefully capture the bat then call the health district at 440-350-2543 to determine if the bat should be tested for rabies, officials said. “Residents should not fear spending time outside, but should be aware and keep their pets nearby,” Health Commissioner Adam Litke is quoted in the release. What is rabies? Rabies is a rare but extremely deadly virus — “virtually 100% fatal” once symptoms appear, according to the World Health Organization . Carriers are typically bats, raccoons, skunks and foxes. An estimated 3 in 4 Americans live in a community where rabid wildlife have been found, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . Though human deaths from rabies are rare — fewer than 10 each year , according to the CDC — bats are responsible for most of the fatal cases in the U.S. Each year, about 100,000 Americans are vaccinated against rabies following an exposure, according to the release. Rabies vaccinations are mandatory for domestic dogs, cats and ferrets that are at least 4 months old — even for indoor pets. A rabid bat may be able to get into a house and infect indoor pets. What are the symptoms of rabies? After exposure, the rabies virus must travel to the brain. This incubation period can last weeks or months. Without vaccination, the virus is nearly always fatal, once symptoms appear. The first symptoms may include: Flu-like illness including weakness, discomfort, fever or headache Discomfort, prickling or an itching sensation where bitten Typically, the disease takes hold two weeks after the initial symptoms. The more well-known symptoms of rabies include: Thirst and hydrophobia — the fear of water Aggressive behavior like thrashing or biting High bond set for suspect in fatal shooting at Put-in-Bay bar early Thursday How to tell if a bat has rabies Not all bats carry rabies, according to the CDC . But the ones that do usually exhibit unusual behaviors: They’re found in the daytime (most bats are nocturnal). They’re found in unusual places like inside a home or on the ground. They can’t fly or it’s easy to approach them. They make contact with humans, whom they typically avoid. Steer clear of any bats acting strangely, since that may be a sign of rabies, the CDC said. news.content: Community Corner Rabid Bat Startles Patrons At San Diego County Restaurant The bat is the 22nd in San Diego County to test positive for rabies this year. | Updated VISTA, CA — San Diego County public health officials are looking for anyone who may have had contact with a rabid bat found Sunday at a Vista restaurant. The bat landed on a table at Yellow Deli Restaurant while a family was eating around 1 p.m., according to the county. Another diner used a towel to collect the bat and brought it to the San Diego Humane Society in Oceanside, which transferred it to the County's Public Health Lab, where it tested positive for rabies. No direct skin contact with the bat has been reported, officials said. Only people who touched or held the bat are considered at risk for rabies exposure. Officials urged anyone who had direct contact with the bat or knows someone who may have to contact a health care provider as soon as possible. Rabies post-exposure treatment is highly effective when given before symptoms begin, but the disease is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. The bat is the 22nd in San Diego County to test positive for rabies this year. In 2025, 21 bats tested positive. Health officials reminded residents not to touch or approach bats or other wildlife. Anyone who comes into contact with a bat should wash the exposed area with soap and seek medical advice. Bats are a common source of rabies in California, though human cases remain rare. The state's most recent human rabies case occurred in 2024 in a Fresno County resident who was exposed to a bat in Merced County, officials said. news.content_original: Community Corner Rabid Bat Startles Patrons At San Diego County Restaurant The bat is the 22nd in San Diego County to test positive for rabies this year. | Updated VISTA, CA — San Diego County public health officials are looking for anyone who may have had contact with a rabid bat found Sunday at a Vista restaurant. The bat landed on a table at Yellow Deli Restaurant while a family was eating around 1 p.m., according to the county. Another diner used a towel to collect the bat and brought it to the San Diego Humane Society in Oceanside, which transferred it to the County's Public Health Lab, where it tested positive for rabies. No direct skin contact with the bat has been reported, officials said. Only people who touched or held the bat are considered at risk for rabies exposure. Officials urged anyone who had direct contact with the bat or knows someone who may have to contact a health care provider as soon as possible. Rabies post-exposure treatment is highly effective when given before symptoms begin, but the disease is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. The bat is the 22nd in San Diego County to test positive for rabies this year. In 2025, 21 bats tested positive. Health officials reminded residents not to touch or approach bats or other wildlife. Anyone who comes into contact with a bat should wash the exposed area with soap and seek medical advice. Bats are a common source of rabies in California, though human cases remain rare. The state's most recent human rabies case occurred in 2024 in a Fresno County resident who was exposed to a bat in Merced County, officials said. Read Full Bio Adam Harrington Updated on: July 23, 2026 / 5:09 PM CDT / CBS Chicago Add CBS News on Google Officials in Kane County, Illinois, warned Thursday that some one-year rabies vaccines administered to pets during county vaccination clinics this year may have lost potency.The rabies vaccines manufactured by Elanco were administered between August and October 2025, according to the Kane County Public Information Office. Since they may have lost potency, they have been recalled.The county emphasized that this does not mean an affected pet has rabies or is otherwise sick. But testing did find the vaccines given last year may not provide protection for a full 12 months as they are supposed to.Elanco has provided Kane County Animal Control with about 400 replacement shots that will be administered free of cost. Kane County Animal Control has also mailed letters to pet owners whose animals got the shots that have now been recalled.Voluntary revaccinations are available by appointment only, the county said. Anyone looking to schedule one should contact Kane County Animal Control at 630-232-3555.The county noted that some of the affected one-year vaccines administered last year expire as early as next month anyway, and Illinois law requires pets to have a current rabies vaccination. analysis.brief_en: Kane County, Illinois officials have recalled some rabies vaccines administered to pets last year due to potential loss of potency. The vaccines, manufactured by Elanco and given between August and October 2025, may not provide the full 12 months of protection as required by Illinois law. While the county stressed that affected pets do not have rabies, they are offering free replacement shots and have contacted pet owners via mail. Pet owners can schedule revaccinations by appointment with Kane County Animal Control. This situation highlights the importance of maintaining up-to-date rabies vaccinations for pets.

(WWSB) - Sarasota County has issued a rabies advisory after an infected racoon was killed near Proctor Road Monday, the Department of Health announced.Officials said the single case of rabies was confirmed after the raccoon was killed on the corner of Grove Point Boulevard and Proctor Road on July 21. “All residents and visitors should be aware that rabies may be currently present in the wild animal population,” the advisory said.People and domestic animals should always avoid physical contact with wild animals including bats, foxes, skunks, otters, bobcats and coyotes, which carry a higher risk of human exposure. Rabies advisory issued in Charlotte County after raccoon tests positiveAnimals with rabies may show strange behavior, the health department says. Infected animals can be aggressive, attacking for no apparent reason, or act very tame (especially wild animals). They may not be able to eat, drink or swallow.They may drool because they are unable to swallow their saliva. They may stagger or become paralyzed. Eventually they will die.If you are exposed to rabies, receiving appropriate treatment after exposure will protect you from the risk of rabies.People can take precautions to prevent rabies exposure:Immunize pets and livestock based on your veterinarian’s recommended schedule.Keep pets under direct supervision and on a leash, and keep livestock secured on your property. If an animal bites your pet or livestock, seek veterinary assistance for the animal immediately and contact Sarasota Animal Services at 941-861-9501.Avoid contact with wild or stray animals. Do not handle, feed, or unintentionally attract them with outdoor pet food, open garbage cans, or other sources of food. If you have been bitten or scratched by a wild or domestic animal, seek medical attention, and report the injury to DOH-Sarasota by calling 941-861-2873.Never adopt wild animals or bring them into your home; instead contact a licensed wildlife rehabilitator.Call your local animal control agency to remove any stray animals from your neighborhood. Contact Sarasota Animal Services at 941-861-9501.Prevent wildlife, including bats, from entering living quarters or occupied spaces in homes, schools, and other similar areas where they might come in contact with people and pets. news.content: Wednesday, July 22, 2026 | Wildlife Rabid Bat Confirmed in Blaine County, Public Health Officials Advise Residents to Take Precautions South Central Public Health District (SCPHD) recently confirmed rabies in a bat on July 14 located in Blaine County, south of Stanley. The case is the first confirmed rabid bat in South Central Idaho this year and serves as a reminder to take extra precautions should you encounter one. The rabies virus can cause a fatal illness in both people and their pets. Although rabies is found only in bats in Idaho, the disease is uncommon, occurring in only about 1% of bats. The virus is spread through the saliva, typically by a bite or scratch. Because it is difficult to determine whether a bat is infected based on its appearance or behavior, people should avoid handling bats and treat any direct contact as a potential exposure. If a person or pet may have been exposed to a live bat, contact your local public health district to determine whether rabies testing or medical treatment is needed. Residents in Lemhi and Custer counties should contact Eastern Idaho Public Health at (208) 533-3152. Blaine County residents should contact South Central Public Health District at (208) 737-5912. As bats begin migrating and preparing for hibernation in the fall, encounters with people and pets can become more common. Give bats plenty of space and avoid disturbing them. If you find a live bat inside your home or another enclosure, please contact the Salmon Regional Office for assistance on safe removal. To protect yourself and pets from rabies: Do not touch a bat with your bare hands. If you come in contact with a bat, seek medical attention. Place the bat in a ventilated (i.e., not airtight if the bat is alive) container while using thick gloves or another method to transfer into a container without touching it with bare skin. Contact your local public health district Always vaccinate your pets, including cats and horses. Pets may encounter bats outdoors or in the home. Bat-proof your home or cabin by plugging all holes in the siding and maintain tight fitting screens on windows. Bats can enter through holes the size of a quarter. To avoid killing dependent young inside the structure, wait to seal outside entrances until after bats are gone in the fall. Sealing gaps on the interior of the structure should be completed immediately and can be safely done anytime. news.content: By Staff Report | editor@news-herald.com | Hartford Courant Staff PUBLISHED: July 24, 2026 at 3:45 PM EDT Getting your Trinity Audio player ready... The Ohio Department of Health recently confirmed Lake County’s first rabid bat since 2022, according to an announcement from the Lake County General Health District. The health district said that the bat was found in a Painesville house. “Humans and pets are exposed to the rabies virus when they are either bitten or scratched by an animal with rabies; or less commonly, when saliva from an infected animal gets into an open wound or mucous membrane,” said LCGHD Environmental Supervisor Bert Mechenbier in the online post. Mechenbier added that if a person is exposed to a bat, “or if a bat is discovered in the house while residents are sleeping,” the bat needs to be “carefully captured.” Residents should call the health department at 440-350-2543 to decide if the bat needs to be tested. “Residents should not fear spending time outside, but should be aware and keep their pets nearby,” said Health Commissioner Adam Litke in the post. Mechenbier added that there are mandatory rabies vaccination laws for dogs, cats and ferrets that are more than 4 months old, including indoor pets. He urged families to ensure the pet vaccinations are up to date. “Vaccinating pets against rabies protects the pet, as well as family members, against the threat of this fatal disease,” the post said. The health district said that more information about rabies can be found from the Ohio Department of Health at odh.ohio.gov or the Centers for Disease Control at cdc.gov/rabies . DEKALB COUNTY, Ga. - Health officials in Decatur issued a public warning after testing confirmed a dead bat carried rabies in southern DeKalb County on Tuesday. What we know: A dead bat recovered near Columbia Drive and York Place in south DeKalb County tested positive for rabies on Tuesday. County workers also reported an infected bat near Millstone Trail in the Stone Mountain area. Officials noted that Georgia is endemic for rabies, meaning the brain-damaging virus circulates naturally among animals all year. What we don't know: Authorities have not stated whether any people or household pets came into direct contact with either bat. It remains unclear if animal control officers have conducted local trappings in response to these cases. What you can do: Residents must vaccinate their pets every year and register the official tags directly with DeKalb County Animal Control. Officials advise homeowners to secure garbage cans, eliminate outdoor pet feeding stations, and keep a close eye on pets for unusual behavior. Anyone bitten or scratched by a wild or strange animal should seek emergency medical attention right away. To report an animal bite or request assistance, call DeKalb County Animal Control at 404-294-2996, extension 2, during weekday hours from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., or dial 404-294-2519 after hours. The backstory: Rabies spreads through saliva, primarily when an infected animal bites another creature or a human. Because the virus occurs regularly across the state, local authorities only trap wild animals if a domestic pet or human suffers a bite or scratch. The Source: The information in this story was gathered from N. Wallen, Animal Enforcement Services Director, who issued official public health alerts through press documentation, as well as the DeKalb County Communications Department. analysis.location_and_population: Nigeria, particularly Abuja and surrounding communities.
analysis.event: The article discusses the ongoing threat of rabies in Nigeria, focusing on the farmer-herder conflict and its impact on public health and safety. It does not report any confirmed rabies cases or outbreaks.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The article highlights the persistent threat of rabies in Nigeria, but no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are reported. The risk is not explicitly stated.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The article does not provide information on specific responses such as investigation, testing, isolation, or contact tracing related to rabies. It is a general discussion on the issue.

analysis.brief_en: The article titled 'Why Rabies Still Threatens Nigerians' by Real Broadcasting Network, published on 2026-07-25, discusses the ongoing threat of rabies in Nigeria. It emphasizes the farmer-herder conflict in Abuja's outskirts as a contributing factor to the persistence of rabies. However, the article does not report any confirmed cases, deaths, or exposures related to rabies. It also does not detail specific responses such as testing, isolation, or contact tracing. The focus is on the broader context of public health challenges and the need for improved community awareness and prevention measures. The content is a general discussion and does not provide explicit risk assessments or operational impacts related to rabies.

news.content: EAST PROVIDENCE, R.I. (WPRI) — On Friday, July 24, the city of Pawtucket announced that two raccoons tested positive for rabies . Around the same time, the state of Rhode Island disclosed that West Nile virus was detected in a mosquito sample collected in Cranston . In this edition of Beyond the Forecast , 12 News Meteorologist Steven Matregrano goes in-depth on both topics. First, he speaks with Dr. Scott Marshall, Rhode Island's state veterinarian, about what rabies is, which species it can affect and what to do if you come across a wild animal. Dr. Jannelle Couret, a mosquito abatement coordinator with the R.I. Department of Environmental Management, then joins the show to explain how to reduce the risk of mosquito-borne illnesses and protect yourself against mosquito bites. LEARN MORE: EEE, West Nile virus: The symptoms and how to protect yourself Locations are not exact and are meant to illustrate findings by community. Haiti - Maritime Scholarships : Call for Applications Haiti - Security : The United States lifts restrictions that limited its cooperation with the FAd'H Haiti - Moscow : Haitian student Slanda François, detained in Russia, released Zapping Haiti of July 24, 2026 more news Donation from Brazil of 10,000 doses of human rabies vaccine Haiti's PM pays tribute to the great figures of Konpa FLASH : Medinel Zamor injured, out of the U-20 Champions League Championship Colombia : Haiti's Mission on cocoa Venezuela : Haiti honors its medical brigade returning from its solidarity mission more news Donation from Brazil of 10,000 doses of human rabies vaccine 25/07/2026 11:02:52 On Thursday, July 22, 2026, the Ministry of Public Health received a donation of 10,000 doses of human rabies vaccine at the PROMESS warehouse. The donation was provided by the Government of Brazil through the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO). The delivery of this significant donation to Haiti was made possible through the joint efforts of PANAFTOSA, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the logistical support of the World Food Programme (WFP), which facilitated the air transport of the vaccines to Port-au-Prince. This donation comes at a time when rabies remains a public health threat in Haiti. Between the first and twenty-fourth epidemiological weeks of 2026, 1,481 attacks by animals suspected of having rabies were reported in the country, including 3 deaths, with the situation remaining concentrated in the Central and Western departments. Although this disease is preventable with prompt treatment after exposure, it is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. Access to rabies vaccines is therefore essential to protect populations exposed to animal bites. Thanks to this contribution from the Brazilian Government, health authorities will have a strengthened stockpile, enabling them to improve the care of people exposed to rabies and support prevention efforts in several departments of the country. This initiative illustrates the importance of regional solidarity and coordinated international cooperation in addressing health challenges. It is part of the ongoing efforts of the Ministry of Public Health and Population (MSPP), with the support of friendly countries like Brazil and the United States, and its partners like the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), to reduce the risk of rabies-related deaths and ensure better access to essential health products. supplementary_news.content_title: Beyond the Forecast: The risk of rabies and mosquito-borne diseases
supplementary_news.content: EAST PROVIDENCE, R.I. (WPRI) — On Friday, July 24, the city of Pawtucket announced that two raccoons tested positive for rabies . Around the same time, the state of Rhode Island disclosed that West Nile virus was detected in a mosquito sample collected in Cranston . In this edition of Beyond the Forecast , 12 News Meteorologist Steven Matregrano goes in-depth on both topics. First, he speaks with Dr. Scott Marshall, Rhode Island’s state veterinarian, about what rabies is, which species it can affect and what to do if you come across a wild animal. Dr. Jannelle Couret, a mosquito abatement coordinator with the R.I. Department of Environmental Management, then joins the show to explain how to reduce the risk of mosquito-borne illnesses and protect yourself against mosquito bites. Locations are not exact and are meant to illustrate findings by community. Source: RI DEM/RI DOH, MA DPH Download the WPRI 12 and Pinpoint Weather 12 apps to get breaking news and weather alerts.
